With respect to conscription or any other subject, the decision depends entirely upon the authority with which a person speaks in dealing with defence needs, the information he is able to present and the charges he is able to prove. I would certainly let the hon. member know my stand then. I would say that defence spending should not be cut down but rather should be decentralized and more money should be spent on buildings and so on in the poorer provinces so they would be able to improve their position and would not have to suffer the stigma of being referred to as the poorer provinces.
If certain provinces have not progressed as expected since the time of confederation, then the fault lies not only with the Liberal party but also with the Conservative party because they are the parties that have held office from time to time and have governed the country. Any development that has not taken place in the maritimes is of course the fault of the policies these two parties have had from time to time, and they are equally to blame.
It is not my intention to discuss the virtues or ill effects of the adoption of the Rowell-Sirois commission report. That has been

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements done on more than one occasion since the report was made, but I would say that so far as dominion-provincial fiscal arrangements are concerned we have actually two alternatives. One is to come to an agreement with respect to the equalization of taxation as is proposed by the minister at this time. Alternatively, and I favour the plan that we should bring about the development of the non-industrial areas of Canada so we will not have such a thing as poorer provinces.
Since 1945 the federal government has been able to look after peacetime, wartime and defence needs. It has reduced the national debt. It has also reduced the income tax level by some 19 per cent since preKorean war days. Yesterday the Minister of Fisheries asked where the money was coming from for the increases we propose with respect to the equalization grants. I think he would agree in this instance that these tax cuts, which were made for election purposes, most notably to serve his own party's ends, certainly did not help the Canadian public very much as such but particularly helped those areas where they had heavy income taxes. These were not the poorer provinces, so it was a case again of giving income tax cuts to those provinces that were not in need of money.
If we are going to follow through the plan of equalization, I feel that it would have been more proper to have kept the rates as they were and to have passed on increased assistance to the provinces through municipal aid and otherwise. As long as private and public investment continues its expansion in this country I contend that the federal government will gain more revenue. That expansion, of course, will increase the gross national product, as I indicated yesterday, and so the government through taxation will feel the effects in its coffers of this increase in the gross national product.
The provinces, of course, have their headaches and I shall probably deal with some of them shortly. The federal government gets the major share of the profits from industrial development through the expansion of corporation taxes and otherwise, and leaves the provinces and more particularly the municipal districts to supply all services such as communication and conservation and development. It is only logical, Mr. Speaker, that the federal government should shoulder a substantial portion of that cost. I would say there is no need for a change in the British North America Act as such. What we need actually is mutual agreement with respect to fiscal responsibility. If we should have a reassessment of responsibility I feel that we could

Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements reach a mutual agreement between the provinces and the federal government, something which is lacking today.
I am one who is opposed to the federal government becoming the caretaker of the provinces. I absolutely disagree with the principle that is involved, namely that the federal government should collect all the taxes and hand them out to the provinces and to the municipal districts to do with as they wish. I say that for the following reason. From time to time we find that those who are given money very freely, as this would apparently be given, have become irresponsible in their methods of handling those funds. While I recognize the fact that the federal government, through the collection of these taxes, simplifies collections and that therefore the Canadian taxpayer will get more for his dollar in so far as the government will receive more, at the same time that advantage would be lost if any irresponsibility were to set in. The proper answer would be the development of the poorer provinces in an effort to bring them up to the standard of the richer provinces.
I contend that the unity of Canada will depend not on non-interference by the federal government in provincial affairs but rather upon federal participation in the development of these provinces. Under the circumstances, because of the lack of development in this country on an equal basis from the maritimes to British Columbia, I must accordingly agree that the need exists for an equalization in taxation to assist these poorer provinces. At the same time I must favour the money being spent for the development of those areas that are not being developed today.
I would say that from an equalization of grants to those provinces it does not necessarily follow that we shall have an equalization of expenditures in those provinces, by reason of the fact that each province has different problems. We have welfare differences in each province. My own province, by way of example, has a health and welfare program which includes a form of health insurance. We also have additional assistance to old age pensioners or senior citizens, whichever you wish to call them, who are in need. We have in the provinces problems that are peculiar to each, such as road building in British Columbia which is much more costly than it would be in Saskatchewan or Prince Edward Island. Each province has the problem of education and the municipal problems peculiar to that province.
There is one place where the federal authority might be of assistance in taking the load from the provinces in this field of


education. If the government were to listen to its member from Victoria, British Columbia, who has from time to time expressed the view that a greater expenditure on technical training would be of inestimable value to the provinces, it would be of assistance. I would say that none of that load ought to be carried by the provinces. The federal authority would not be interfering with education by developing the field of technical training, in view of the fact that there is such a need in this country today for such trained people. We have the problems of conservation peculiar to each province, such as the forest production in my own province as compared with other provinces such as Prince Edward Island. We have the agricultural problems in Saskatchewan and Prince Edward Island as compared with the manufacturing production of Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia. There is the problem of resource development, and the lack of natural resources which is apparent in some of these poorer provinces. We do have specific centralization of population and industry in certain provinces which causes an imbalance, as I see it, within the nation itself. This makes it impossible for these poorer provinces to develop as I feel they should develop. We have the problem of marketing as it applies to each individual province.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I maintain it is a responsibility of the government of Canada to develop Canada on a more equitable basis and so prevent the federal government from becoming a caretaker government. It is my contention that if this government were to expend some of its surplus in the development of areas that are today considered the poorer provinces, eventually those provinces would reach a point where they would no longer be so considered, thereby doing away with the need for this parliament to continually revise the tax agreements with the various provinces. The equalization grants as I consider them, mean that a certain amount of this money is being poured down the drain. As I have indicated at other times, there are only so many dollars available from the Canadian taxpayer, and those dollars should be utilized to the greatest advantage of each province in Canada.
In closing I can only urge that this government use some of the surpluses it has from time to time through the growth of the country and the increase in the gross national product for the extension of technical training, for industrial development and to make funds available through the industrial bank to secondary industry to a greater extent

than it is today; to develop power and resources in the various provinces that have no such resources and power available, and to the utilization of our natural resources to the absolute maximum.
If this government follows through with the tax agreement program I am satisfied that five years from now we shall be asked to discuss once again a program of equalization grants for the provinces. In any event this bill should not be passed until such time as we have some indication from the provinces that they are prepared to accept it.

The tendency toward increasing centralization is something that has to be watched, but I shall leave that to the experts. However, the second point-and this is the point we actually have to face up to-that I should like to touch on is what, for want of a better name, I have called the dollars and cents aspect of it.
This legislation has been said to be necessary, of course, to provide a reasonable level of provincial services without an abnormal burden of taxation. I think those are the words of the Prime Minister in letters to the premiers, and they are also already on the record.
I want to take a minute to indicate some of the onerous taxation burdens borne by the province of New Brunswick. I think these are facts and figures which have not yet been brought to the attention of this house. First of all I should like to refer to our problem in connection with education, and the financing we must do in New Brunswick. A royal commission sat last year which dealt quite extensively with the problem of school financing. It was found that the people of New Brunswick spend a higher proportion of their personal income on education than do the people of any other Canadian province, 3-9 per cent in the last recorded year as against 2-7 per cent for Ontario and 2-8 per cent for Canada generally. Of course I could go on to point out how that disparity is increased because our personal income is lower.
This royal commission noted that whereas New Brunswick has 4-4 per cent of Canada's school enrolment it has only 2-2 per cent of Canada's income. Ontario with 32 per cent of the total school enrolment has 40 per cent of Canada's income. New Brunswick lacks educationally because it lacks economically. Then we are faced with the shocking fact that although New Brunswick is making the biggest effort of any province to provide proper educational facilities, it falls far short of the mark.
In that respect I should like to refer to sets of figures which have already been put on the record. First of all is the statement by the leader of the C.C.F. party, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), who gave the per capita personal income by provinces. It was shown that in 1954 New

The Minister of Finance and other government spokesmen speaking in support of this legislation contend that it is designed to meet the need for some reallocation of revenues, and to assist the various governments to meet their financial responsibilities. Other members of this party, and other members in the house, have dealt with the question as to whether or not this bill goes any distance in enabling the various governments to cope with those responsibilities. It seems to me, as one who has listened to this debate both at the resolution stage and on second reading, that there is a forgotten Canadian so far as this bill and these arrangements are concerned. I refer to our old age pensioners.
I make no apology, Mr. Speaker, for mentioning old age pensions in connection with this bill; for government spokesmen themselves, in their effort to persuade parliament and the country that the federal government is doing something magnanimous toward the provinces, have drawn attention repeatedly to the amount of money that goes from the federal treasury toward old age pensions and other forms of social security.
We in this group are proud of the extent to which Canada has moved in the direction of social security. We are proud of the fact, and we believe we played some part in it, that some of our social security at any rate has been established on a basis of universality. We hope the day will come when we will have an over-all social security program based on that principle of universality, so that all Canadians will have certain guarantees which we believe are their right because of the contribution that all Canadians make to the economy and well-being of this country.

The U.F.A. government, which up to that time had done a good job in Alberta, was simply forced into the position in which it was unable to raise the money it needed.
This is the next important thing to get in mind. The U.F.A., as part of what they thought a good method of financing, had adopted the policy of selling Alberta savings certificates. You are not dealing with the Social Credit now, so don't lie about it. The U.F.A. had sold these savings certificates. A savings certificate was a promise on the part of the government to pay a certain amount of money on demand with interest at 4 per cent. Just get what I am saying. It is not easy to get these facts, anyway. The province of Alberta would borrow $100 from a man just as though he put $100 on deposit in the provincial treasury. It would agree to pay that $100 back when he demanded it, and would agree to pay him 4 per cent interest on that money until he demanded it. That is simple; anybody can see that. It was good business, because 4 per cent interest was a great deal less than Alberta had to pay for money on the money market. Altogether the U.F.A. had borrowed from the people of Alberta $10 million in that form. In other words there was outstanding $10 million of Alberta savings certificates. Once more remember that Social Credit had not come in at that time.

While we from the western provinces do disagree, sometimes on the basis of partisanship, nonetheless when the welfare of the western provinces is being discussed and in particular when our major subject, agricultural production, is being discussed, we bury our disagreements and unite for the common benefit of the western provinces. Sometimes, as I listened to my hon. friends from the maritimes upholding those things which they themselves assuredly cannot support other than vocally, I wonder

I do not want to go far afield in order to call evidence in support of the strength of the arguments he advanced and the power of the analogy he drew as to the differences between the maritimes and elsewhere, but I think I should call as evidence an editorial in the Toronto Daily Star of last evening, a newspaper which throughout the years has never been too prone to criticism of the government except during the present session in so far as the preservation of the parliamentary system is concerned. Yesterday the Daily Star dealt with thi; question at length, and no one supporting the government will be able to say I am quoting from a newspaper that at any time has shown antagonism to this government. The subject of the editorial is, "Why Dominion-Provincial Tax Fight is Your Business". It sets out in detail quite a lengthy analysis of what actually is the essence of this bill, and it ends up in this way:
Is there any satisfactory alternative to double taxation in Ontario and perhaps other provinces?
It is generally following the viewpoint of Ontario in that question, but it mentions other provinces. The answer it gives is, I think, an effective argument in support of what the hon. member for Saint John-Albert said this morning, and an equally effective answer to the arguments advanced by the hon. member for Charlotte. The answer given is as follows:
The only alternative is for Ottawa to allow the provinces a larger share of income and corporation taxes. In the Star's opinion this is not only desirable in the case of Ontario but is essential in the case of the maritime provinces particularly.
I once more underline and emphasize those words; an increased amount of income and corporation taxes made available to certain provinces, and in particular in the maritime provinces, is essential. It refers to the maritime provinces particularly, and generally to the other provinces.
Unless they receive a larger share of the national wealth they will continue to be second class Canadians, economically speaking.

Call it a constitutional convention, if you like, without the power of amendment of the constitution in respect of those fundamental rights which are inherent in the constitution, but why not have a gathering designed to bring about the reconsideration of a problem which for the last 13 years or so has become increasingly complex?
When I go back to 1945 I remember the great hopes that were held; and I am in agreement with my hon. friend the minister in this regard that the matter is complex. It is one of the most difficult problems that parliament, or the government, can be called upon to deal with, because there are so many facets, so many difficulties and so many situations that demand not an arbitrary attitude but a compromising and a considered one.

The question was asked of the Prime Minister, do the recommendations or suggestions in the green book exist anly longer? The answer was no. That is not the attitude, that is not the consideration to which the provinces are entitled under a constitution which allocates powers as between the federal and provincial governments. That is not an attitude which will remove the road blocks which today deny Canada the development which should indeed be hers. I feel that even yet if there were an attitude on the part of the federal government to negotiate, terms could be achieved which would be acceptable and which would go a long way toward solving this difficult and complex problem.

Whoever drafted this bill deserves high commendation for his powers of draftsmanship. The terms are difficult and intricate. This bill and the offer made by the government at the last conference constitute a political mixture. We have the carrot and the club. The government is dangling before the provinces less than is needed by the provinces, less than they can possibly and justifiably carry out their responsibilities with, and on the other hand is saying, "If you do not take it, then what?" It is the carrot and the club. That is not the attitude that brought about confederation; that is not a concept

I am going to deal with the situation from the point of view of the provinces other than Ontario and Quebec. Quebec stands to gain very materially, as it receives immediately an assured $40 million. What is going to happen to the provinces? What of education? What of increased demands for highways and other development in the various provinces which inevitably bring benefit to the dominion government? The attitude of the dominion government toward the municipalities has been unfair and unjust. I have only to go back to a motion which was before this house on April 30 and May 1 providing for something for which the municipalities have been asking, that the dominion government should follow the lead of two provincial governments and pay taxation upon its own industries and upon its own public buildings in the various municipalities. The government went part of the way but did not go far enough.
Why should the municipal authorities be required to provide the necessary services in the way of roads and so on for federal government institutions without that government paying full taxation? Why should the municipalities be required to pay 10 per cent sales tax on their needs, apart from the exceptions in connection with fire and road machinery costing over $1,000 per unit? Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements You take it or leave it." This is the law of the feudal lord to the vassals. The vassals must accept because of the exigencies of the financial responsibilities which exist.
In this changing world in which we live, wherein the communists place their emphasis on scientific training and technological education, there must be some responsibility placed on the federal government if Canada and the other free nations are to be able to take their place in our world today. Let us deal for just a moment with what has happened in the last five years in connection with primary and secondary education. The school population of Canada has gone up from 2-5 million to 3 [DOT] 5 million, and there are 97 per cent more pre-school age children today than there were in 1941. The provinces cannot discharge their responsibilities in assisting the municipalities in this regard. If you are going to leave that responsibility on the municipality and no change is made in the content of this bill, the result will be that in the very near future you will have a strong dominion government with bankrupt municipalities. If the government will not listen to this argument which I am advancing, will they listen to the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre if he whispers that to them today? That view has been expressed by the hon. member over and over again.
What about the universities? What about the salaries paid in the universities? The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) is the chancellor of one of our great universities and no doubt has had experience with the magnetic pull by industry, government and business in so far as his teaching staff is concerned. Other universities have felt this. Dr. Smith of the University of Toronto has pointed out the great difficulty there is in this regard.
What assistance has been given to university education? There have been a few scholarships, a few research scholarships. The extent of assistance to the universities has been insufficient to meet the completely changing conditions that prevail today. You will not achieve the success with your five-year plan that Stalin had in mind when he instituted his five-year plan. You will have bankruptcy at the end for the municipalities of this country unless some assistance is forthcoming.
What about university salaries? President Sidney Smith has stated that the University of Toronto is losing personnel to government, industry and research because the salaries are two or three times what the university can afford to pay. Do you realize that the average Canadian worker has increased his wages two-thirds over the past generation,
6372	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements but the salary oi the average teacher and research worker has remained unchanged?
Those are not my views. Those are the views of the Canadian association of university teachers. Thousands of the mentally gifted youth are barred from higher education by financial limitations. Are we going to restrict our universities by the financial assistance extended to the provinces today, or are we going to realize now that the U.S.S.R. has departed from its old policy of being a stolid introvert and has become a smiling extrovert that goes all over the world expanding its technological and educational system? Are we in the free world going to fall behind? Are we going to deny admission to the universities to all except those who are well to do? That is what is going to happen.
The United States sends to university seven times as many, in proportion to population, as we do. The U.S.S.R. sends far more than we do to that type of education, which is necessary in the world today as we enter this new atomic era. There is no way whereby the vast demand for engineers, scientists and mathematicians can be met other than by this dominion government extending itself as it has not done before and providing grants in aid, while maintaining the constitutional position whereby the provinces are in charge of education.
Sir, all you have to do is look at the record, the roster of engineers and scientists iri the U.S.S.R. Do you say that they lag behind us and we do not need to increase our efforts? Within the past few days on July 19, John E. Bird, Canadian Press staff writer, referred to an interview he had with Dr. Lloyd G. Elliott, director of the physics division of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, following the latter's return from a conference in the Russian capital May 14 to 22. This is what Dr. Elliott said:
We In Canada knew very little about what Russia was doing in the field before the conference. We came away realizing that Soviet scientists are making real progress. . . . They are very serious and their plans are very extensive for placing large numbers of highly technical people in basic research.
We go on in the same old way, with 290 or so scholarships. What does the U.S.S.R. do? Here is the latest record. The United States has 108,700 engineers; the seven countries in western Europe making up NATO have 111,000; the Soviet union has 540,000. All over the world today they are loaning these technical advisers who, through the knowledge they possess, infiltrate in those countries and thereby secure an exchange, on the part of the freedom-loving people of those countries, of their freedom


for all time in return for basic technical knowledge. The United States has 4,200 agricultural scientists; the seven countries in western Europe have 21,245; the Soviet union has 190,000. The United States has 6,100 mathematicians; the Soviet union has 160,000.
Make all due allowances, Mr. Speaker, for the impelling virtue that freedom gives to men and women, whether it is in the ordinary field of life or in science. The universities face a serious crisis and this bill in no way meets the situation. It simply places upon the provinces the handcuffs of five years of inaction in this direction, for they have gone as far as they can. I say to you, sir, and to the Prime Minister through you, that this is a field that must be entered by the dominion government as part of our national defence, failing which we shall lose the next five years under this five-year plan. We shall unless something else is done. We must act now if we are to maintain and preserve our position as a freedom-loving nation in the world. We must also accelerate our contribution to scientific technology and mathematical knowledge and technique everywhere in the world.
How far they have gone in the U.S.S.R. is shown by one other statistic. It was brought to Canada by Mr. James S. Duncan of the Massey-Harris company, when he said that so intent has the U.S.S.R. become on increasing the sum total of scientific knowledge that of the 40,000 workers in the Stalin works in Moscow, 10,000 in their after hours are taking courses which in five or six years will graduate them as engineers.
I do not want anyone to say that I want Canada to borrow the means of communism in order to defeat communism. However, I believe that if we in this country on the national level will give to the various universities not the paltry sums advanced today but sums in keeping with the responsibilities that rest upon those universities in this new world we shall not only ensure Canada's contribution to the maintenance of freedom, but we shall also make possible a university education for many tens of thousands of young people in our country who otherwise would be denied the opportunity of a university education which their ability and capacity would merit and which only their inability to finance would deny.
That is one phase of the picture; another phase is in connection with national development. I am not going to go extensively into that-it has been covered over and over again during the progress of this debate-but I wish to point out two matters of national import which we in Saskatchewan believe are deserving of, and indeed demand, dominion support. One of them, which was

dealt with by several hon. members, is the need to realize that whilst highways are under the constitution a matter of provincial administration, to a greater degree than heretofore there must be grants in aid; for the present bill, if implemented, will make it impossible for provinces to expand their necessary highway development.
We have recognized the principle in connection with the trans-Canada highway, although the rate at which the trans-Canada highway is being built shows a pedestrian drive behind that worthy objective. Through the municipalities my own province of Saskatchewan, as well as other provinces, is asking that there be a realization that while at the time of confederation east and west roads were of first importance, today in the national interest there must be highways for defence in the various provinces. To that end federal assistance must be given. The provinces will never discharge their responsibility in this regard if hemmed in, as they will be, by the ambit of the terms of the present bill.
The demand for highways of that kind has some foundation in history. In 1912 both Sir Wilfrid Laurier and Sir Robert Borden supported federal aid to highways necessary for development. In 1920 the government of Right Hon. Arthur Meighen brought into effect a system of assistance which, as I recall it, involved the spending of some $20 million. There must be some assistance in this regard. Who gets the benefit of the highway into the north? As soon as the highway is built and minerals are found, mines are opened and smelters are constructed, the dominion government immediately takes its Cut. It takes it before in the sales tax. It achieves dividends immediately.
These highways are necessary for development. Indeed, I believe that a roads to resources program of assistance by the federal government would meet with general approval across the country, roads to resources, the opening up of the country, and those roads available later as defence highways if and when needed. I know that such a program would meet with approval in the western provinces. The United States has launched one of the greatest highway programs in all history. It is one that requires co-operation on the part of the states of the United States. In it the federal authority, with the administration resting upon the states, has launched one of the greatest moves in all history to assure that development which highways permit and, indeed, encourage.
Those are but two fields: education, highways and encouragement of national development, which will not be encouraged to

I said a moment ago that it is better than what has been given previously but it still constitutes a failure to realize that under our constitution the provinces were never intended to be beggars. The provinces have responsibilities, the provinces have fields of action, and the concentration of power and authority in the federal government with respect to taxation has had an adverse effect.
The bill will go some way toward removing those adverse effects, but unless the amounts to be paid to the several provinces are materially enhanced by grants in aid of education and by a system whereby the municipalities may be assured of a reasonable opportunity to discharge their responsibilities, then indeed, looking ahead five years, the provinces having to accept the terms of the bill will mean that the bill will have an adverse effect on the municipalities and their responsibilities and will adversely interfere with Canada's international responsibilities in the field of technical education to a degree that can never be gained back.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this, I believe, is the first occasion on which I have ever spoken in the house on any matter which was not directly related to my own ministerial responsibilities. It is in a sense a maiden speech, and I crave your indulgence accordingly. It is a very hard thing to be asked to follow so eloquent and persuasive a speaker as the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker). I have no eloquence. I can only try to deal with facts, and I intend to do two things that have been conspicuously absent during most of this debate. I intend to deal as far as possible with facts, and I intend to deal with the bill.
The hon. member for Prince Albert talked about the arbitrary attitude of the government, and several members of the opposition have said the same thing. I think perhaps it might be worth while to take just a minute to consider what really has happened with respect to these proposals. Nothing would have been simpler than for the government to go on as we did in 1952 and recommend that we continue the tax rental agreements, perhaps with some slight change in the formula, and continue the situation which had persisted since 1945, a situation which I submit was not good for this country and which could not much longer continue, whereby the benefits of this legislation were going to two-thirds of the country and not to the other third. That is no way, if we can find a remedy, to allow things to continue.
6374	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements
What did the Prime Minister do? He said that we were going to stick to our one objective that was paramount above all others, and that was to put the provinces on a basis of relative equality, but that we were not at all wedded to the means of tax rental agreements if something better could be found. It was suggested to the provincial governments that if any of them could suggest something better we would be only too happy to consider it. Four conferences were held to discuss various phases of this question, three before an offer was made and one after the offer was made. That was the conference in April which several hon. gentlemen opposite have sought, perhaps unwittingly, to give the impression was the only conference held. It was not.
The views of all the provincial governments were very carefully considered in one stage or another for over a year before these proposals were finally made. If there is going to be legislation there does have to be a point where something becomes final. You cannot bring in a bill that has nothing in it. You have to take a position; and the moment you do take that position it is, of course, very easy for someone else to call it arbitrary. But that does not make it arbitrary at all. The question is this. Does it accomplish what it sets out to accomplish? As I apprehend it, the purpose of this bill is to do two things, and two things only. It is to bring the income of the rest of the provinces up to the level of the combined income of Ontario and British Columbia in three tax fields, or rather the average of the combined revenues of those provinces. That is the prime purpose of the bill. What the government has said is that we feel that all the provinces are entitled to derive in one way or another as much revenue as they would get if they had a taxable capacity comparable to the taxable capacity of the two wealthiest provinces combined. With a scheme like that, it is not intended to raise money for provincial purposes generally. It is only intended to bring the less fortunate provinces up to the level of the more fortunate provinces. This bill does not purport to do anything else and it has nothing to do with anything else, except one thing, and that one thing is an extremely important thing too.
During the war we had the experience of having the wartime tax agreements and I think most Canadians came to the conclusion that it was much more convenient to have only one income tax and only one income tax collector. We are proposing to make that possible if the provincial governments want that; they do not have to take it at all; there is no "take it or leave it" business about it
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

at all; the provincial governments can do exactly as they please about having a single income tax. That is true of every province, and no province loses its equalization payment by doing so. If they want to impose a standard tax, we are prepared to collect it for them. If they want to make a tax rental agreement and accept the yield of the standard tax, we are offering them that. If they prefer to have nothing to do with us and to collect their own taxes at any rate they like, they are still entitled to the equalization payments. It is very hard for me to conceive-and it was evidently quite impossible for any of the provincial governments to conceive-any further modification of this scheme that could have been put into effect; and indeed none of them suggested any. It seems to me that there is a great deal of validity in what Mr. Mackenzie King said in 1935 in that quotation which the hon. member for Eglinton cited yesterday. I do not think there would be any argument at all; not the slightest argument; that not one five-cent piece-and I use the term advisedly-should be collected by the federal treasury in order to be handed over to any provincial government if all the provinces had an equal taxable capacity.

There is only one other point I want to deal with, and it was also raised by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) and in a somewhat different fashion by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell). I took down as completely as I could the words used by the hon. member for Prince Albert. He said that under this bill the maritimes- and by that I assumed he meant the Atlantic provinces-will find themselves in a position less than fair, less than reasonable and less than just. He then suggested that in some way those of us who represent the Atlantic provinces are less good at "ganging up" on the federal treasury than are the gentlemen who represent the western provinces. The only alternative-

The whole purpose of this bill and of this scheme is to achieve equalization. The larger the share of the field that is given to the provinces to tax, the better it is for Ontario but the worse it is for the poorer provinces.

Until the chips are down you could not expect any of the provincial premiers to say he was satisfied with the amount he was going to get. Mr. Smallwood continued:
No other province needs them more for provincial purposes.
I echo that, and I believe we need them in Newfoundland even more than New Brunswick does.
We entered confederation in 1949 on the understanding that we could share on a fair basis the proceeds of income and corporation taxes and succession duties collected all over Canada.
The only way we can share these proceeds on anything iike the same basis as Canadians in the wealthier provinces is by sharing them through the federal treasury.
And that is true of every one of the provinces, except possibly British Columbia and Ontario.
The income and corporation tax fields in Newfoundland, no matter how assiduously we cultivate them, cannot be made to yield the kind of revenues that are secured by the wealthy provinces like Ontario and Quebec.
And yet the 400,000 additional consumers in Newfoundland, who buy nearly everything they consume from the mainland of Canada,-
I might add, mostly from Ontario.
-are contributing every day to the incomes from which income and corporation taxes can be collected in the other provinces, particularly Ontario and Quebec.
It is, therefore, in our provincial interest in Newfoundland and it is in the provincial interest of all the provinces where the tax potential is low, to safeguard the federal share of these tax fields, so that the federal government will be in a position to share them with us. That is the only way all Canadians can finance something approaching provincial services that Ontario can provide out of taxes collected within the province.
The premier of Ontario, at these conferences, has said a good deal about the immense demands for provincial services resulting from the vast industrial expansion of Ontario. Of course, these demands are very large, but the capacity to pay for them grows even faster. I can assure the premier of Ontario that all of us in the Atlantic provinces-
I am sure the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) will agree with this, -would be glad to take on these new provincial liabilities along with the even greater new assets that come with them.
The premier of Ontario and the provincial treasurer have, at these conferences and elsewhere, hinted that Ontario is approaching the end of its fiscal resources. I am sure they don't really expect


the premiers of some of the other provinces to be greatly impressed by their parade of poverty.
The provincial services in Newfoundland, measured in terms of roads or schools or health facilities, or by almost any other standard, do not compare at all with those in Ontario, and it will take many millions of dollars, as our brief to the Gordon commission showed, to bring them up to anything like a comparable basis.
And yet to pay for what we now nave, we in Newfoundland have to impose a gasoline tax of 17 cents, compared with a tax of 11 cents in Ontario. We also have a 3 per cent social security tax on retail sales in the province-and that's on all foodstuffs, too.
I asked our officials to calculate how much more revenue Ontario would be able to collect if the people of Ontario had to pay, for provincal services, taxes which Canadians in the province of Newfoundland have to pay for services which are not nearly as good. I am told that, if Ontario raised its gasoline tax to the rate we have in Newfoundland, it could have collected in 1955 at least an additional 50 million dollars, and that a 3 per cent tax on retail sales in Ontario would have produced at least 150 million dollars in 1955.
That, I might say, is about five times the total budget of Newfoundland.
The fact is that, even with the proposed equalization payments, almost every province in Canada is going to have to continue imposing upon its people much heavier provincial taxation than is borne by the people of Ontario.
As I understand it, under the new tax sharing proposals, Ontario, with standard rates of taxes, will derive substantially more revenue than it would under a continuation of the present tax rental agreements. In other words, the new arrangement will give Ontario a proportionately higher gain than any other province will have.
If the equalization payments were based on the average of the four highest provinces instead of the basis proposed by the federal government,-
That was what Mr. Frost suggested should be done.
-the effect, as I understand it, would be that tax rates would have to be set which would give Ontario a still larger share of the yield from these taxes in order to give the other six provinces payments equal to those proposed in the present federal scheme.
In other words, averaging the top four provinces instead of the top two would give far greater advantages to the wealthy provinces than it would to those with smaller tax potentials.
It is impossible for us from Newfoundland to see how this could possibly be in the national interest, and we cannot help but feel that, by reducing drastically the share the federal treasury would get out of these national tax fields, we would be weakening its capacity to help provide reasonably equal provincial services right across Canada.
And that, sir, is what we understood we would get when we entered confederation in 1949.
And that is what this bill is seeking to continue on a much better basis than we have had it before. That is why I, sir, am only too happy to be supporting it.
I say, therefore, that from the point of view of Newfoundland, and I believe in the interests of at least all the people in the six provinces which the premier of Ontario would not include in his

averaging, his suggestion is much less satisfactory than the suggestion put forward by the federal government.
I feel, to, sir, that we should not forget that the federal government is providing millions for costly services, not merely in Newfoundland and Nova Scotia, but also in Ontario and British Columbia.
That is why we have come to the conclusion-
I wish the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) were in the house to hear this.

Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take up too much of the hon. members' time, but I want to express my personal opinion on the bill before us.
It was the aim of the confederation to unite the provinces, but without unifying them. It seems, moreover, that the fathers of confederation did not so much seek to unite the provinces themselves. Beyond the provincial borders of the day and those that would be established thereafter, they could see the two great races that formed Canada's population at that time and which make it up now, to a considerable extent. They wanted to bring together, not so much the political frameworks as the two ethnical components within those frameworks, to enable them to strive together more efficiently towards a common goal, while satisfying themselves that each of the two would conserve its own identity and would pursue its development according to its own racial characteristics.
In support of this contention I would like to quote an important statement which can be found in the brief presented by the University of Montreal to the Tremblay commission, in February 1952.
There are some who take no pleasure in hearing it said that confederation was a compact between two races .	.	. Any objective and unbiased
examination of the Canadian constitution immediately points to the peculiar status granted to Quebec. Section 133 could hardly be clearer. Provisions relating to language and to the right to the use of it . . . show that the act was really a compact between two racial groups differing in language, religion and traditions, which both were bent on preserving.
Here is, moreover, a statement made at the time of confederation by an expert who, speaking from a neutral point of view, was no doubt in a position to express an objective and unbiased view. This view was
6378	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements expressed by Lord Carnarvon and may be found in the proceedings of the imperial parliament for 1867, page 568:
Lower Canada is deeply attached to its particular institutions and it will join the union only on the clear understanding that it will keep them . . . It is in that spirit and at those conditions that Lower Canada now agrees to enter confederation.
Well, what are those particular institutions, if not our language, our faith, our traditions, our way of thinking, our way of life, of looking after our educational and health needs, and so on?
There is no doubt that the fathers of confederation took a right view of things, even though the means they put at our disposal to achieve their objective were not perfect and have thus, in time, given rise to the difficult situations that are facing us today.
However, because the Canadian nation has developed and progressed to a point that could no doubt be envisioned 90 years ago, and because of a similar change in the economic and social conditions under which this progress is to continue, it might be time to revise this agreement of 1867. It would be advisable to amend it, to clarify it and to adapt it to the new conditions, to draw from it certain practical conclusions which are potentially to be drawn from it and to interpret some of its clauses. Of course, this should be done at a round table discussion to which all interested parties would be invited, namely, the ten provinces and the central government. In other words, it would be the revival and the continuation of the federal-provincial conference held in Quebec in the fall of 1950. That conference, opened and adjourned under the most favourable auspices, had given rise to the fondest hopes. It was to have been resumed and, without blaming anyone in particular, I am very sorry that it was not and that we missed this splendid opportunity to streamline a constitution which no longer answers the needs of the institutions it governs. A further conference could have reassigned to each interested party its own field of taxation, and could have done this more adequately than by the bill now under review.
This task is an essential one, one which will have to be undertaken some time, to bring order and good understanding into intergovernmental relations in Canada. It is in that spirit, no doubt, that the Quebec chamber of commerce, in its submission to the royal inquiry commission in January 1954, made this statement:


In order to amend the British North America Act and to provide Canada with a new constitution, the proceedings of the federal-provincial conference held in Quebec in September 1950 should be resumed as soon as possible.
Such a conference could also settle the equalization problem for which a one-sided solution is offered in Bill 442. I say it is a one-sided solution because there is no evidence that the provinces, which are at least as much interested in this as the central government, were in a position to have their views accepted, even if they were consulted. I do not object on principle to the richer provinces helping the poorer provinces, but I doubt that the way which is contemplated is the best.
Why, for instance, would the central government not encourage each province to levy its own tax on individual and corporation income, by granting not a uniform and partial deduction of 10 per cent of the federal tax, but rather a deduction equal to the full amount collected by the province? Each province would establish its own tax according to a schedule which would best meet the needs and wishes of its people. Such amount being fully deducted from the federal tax, the taxpayers would, in the end, pay the same amount of tax, whatever the variations may be between two provinces. In that way, for instance, the autonomy of Quebec would be preserved. The government of that province has found it advisable to set at a higher level than that of the central government the basic income above which taxes begin to be levied, thus protecting in a more equitable and social way, I think, the family group.
It is obvious, I think, that in such a way the spirit and the word of the constitution would be complied with as far, at least, as paragraph 2 of section 92 is concerned.
I foresee serious objections to the suggestion I am making but, nonetheless, I hold that a conference such as the one held in 1950 would be capable of dealing with those objections, by setting, for instance, a maximum which the provinces could not exceed for a certain period of time.
The constitution irrevocably assigned to the provinces certain fields in which they have the exclusive right to legislate, and that right implies the right to administer. Now then, administration requires the levying of taxes.
Among the fields assigned to the provinces, there are those, among several others, of education and health. Those are, of course.

sacred fields to which the problems of money must be adapted, and not vice versa.
At present, the central government is offering provinces a joint health plan.
In all earnestness, I believe that the province of Quebec should not be put in a position where it should have to accept such a plan. Legislation of this type should be enacted by its own legislature. However, to achieve this object, the bill now under discussion should go even farther than it does, and should allow full deductibility with regard to the amount of the provincial tax, instead of allowing only 10 per cent of the federal tax.
In the field of education, the same situation prevails. In spite of considerable improvement over the last few years, there is still a great deal to be done. We need more revenue. We intend to preserve control of these sources of revenue and be free to use them in the way best suited to the mentality, habits and customs of our people.
We fear that some day the intrusion of the central power in this field may bring about a situation dangerous to our racial group.
I wish to repeat here what I have already said many times before this outside the house. I am not worried about the intrusion or the activities of the present government, headed as it is now by the present Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent). I am not worried either by the possible influence of a government which would be headed by the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew). But who knows what the future holds in store?
What will be the intentions of the men governing the Canadian nation 25 or 50 years from now?
I therefore believe that it is essential today to prepare for the future and to protect it against possible dangers in this field. That is why we should strive to protect and guarantee provincial autonomy.
It seems to me that this measure, imperfect though it is, is a step in the right direction. I feel bound to support it and, in so doing, I believe I interpret the opinion of the truly nationalist independents of the province of Quebec.

The contention of the Minister of Finance is found at page 5988 of Hansard where he says this:
While the tax rental agreements now in their tenth and final year have gone a long way toward meeting these objectives,-
The series of objectives which the minister outlined earlier in his speech.
-in some ways they do not meet all the criteria to which some provinces attach particular Importance. The proposals Incorporated In this bill are designed to reconcile as far as possible these various conflicting points of view.
I quote that particular section because there has been on the part of the government a tendency to fail to appreciate the argument that we of the opposition made respecting tax rental agreements. We have put up a strenuous fight for an equitable reallocation of taxing and service responsibilities between
6382	HOUSE OF
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements the various levels of government. It is a source of encouragement to note that that fight has had the effect at least of carrying the government thus far in changing its mind. By continuing the fight we hope that we might be able to bring the government to a full sense of appreciation of what the essential nature of this difficulty is. In his remarks the Minister of Finance has suggested that he is almost on the point of seeing the light. I quote, for example, the portion of his remarks where he emphasizes the principle- and I am dealing with principle now-of this legislation. The Minister of Finance used the phrase that men and times change. That is quite true, change is a continuous process in the affairs of men. But I should like to add to that phrase used by the minister that principles never change, in this case, principles as they are related to our federal structure of government in Canada. It is a fundamental principle that there must be autonomous areas in both levels of government if our federal system is to survive.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) seems to have an appreciation of this because in his statement at the resolution stage he said, as reported on page 5987 of Hansard for July 16, 1956:
The federal government is not the creature of the provinces, nor are the provinces creatures of it. Each has its own assigned responsibilities,-
It seems to me that there is the fundamental point of objection, at least it is a fundamental point of objection to the present measure so far as my own personal viewpoint is concerned.
I could quote from authorities other than the Minister of Finance in support of this essential principle. The late Mr. Mackenzie King was also a great exponent of the same principle, and in Hansard for 1930, volume II, page 1237, when this matter of giving assistance to the provincial governments was a burning issue because of the depressed economic conditions prevailing, Mr. King had this to say:
When on a previous occasion we were discussing this matter of grants from one treasury to another, I said I thought it was an unsound principle; in fact, I think I used the expression that it was a vicious principle-
I underscore that word "vicious".
-to have one body raise the taxes and another body spend the people's moneys thus raised.
So we have it from the responsible minister in the current Liberal government as well as the gentleman who was the leader of that government for so very long that they recognized the principle that is at stake in this particular issue.
Now, the reason I am taking the trouble to raise this point at the present time is that in


certain quarters of the Liberal party, particularly in Manitoba, there is a failure to appreciate the issue which is at stake. I recall when we were discussing the renewal of the tax rental agreements in 1952 and particularly during the election in 1953, the opposition's stand was misunderstood or misinterpreted deliberately in relation to this problem. I repeat that our stand on that occasion has been vindicated now by the Minister of Finance in the quotation I read where he says that they were merely temporary, that they were merely a passing solution to a very grievous and difficult problem and something better would have to be found. That is precisely the point we, as an opposition, made at that time.
A pamphlet that was circulated in Manitoba, and to which I took rather forceful exception, presented our stand on this matter in 1953 as an election issue. I think I could best bring it to the attention of the house by quoting from the interpretation that was given by the Manitoba Liberals to the Conservative stand at that time. I take the trouble to deal with this subject because I am quite sure that the same misinterpretation will be made of the present stand of the official opposition. The pamphlet, which is a rather rare pamphlet now because I think it must have found its way into the waste-paper basket as fast as it was delivered to those to whom it was directed, is an election pamphlet and it says something to this effect: The Liberal candidate supports the tax rental agreements but his Conservative opponent for Brandon-Souris supports Mr. Drew in his opposition to the dominion-provincial tax agreements and voted with Mr. Drew on his motion of censure reported in unrevised Hansard page 881, December 17, 1952.
Now, I turn to that Hansard and this is what I voted for, and I leave it to all hon. members whether it was a fair interpretation of the stand we took at that time. It was a Conservative amendment to the speech from the throne and there were several sections. Section (e) under question said the following as reported in volume I, page 33 of Hansard for 1952-53:
(e) to reach agreement with the provincial governments in regard to a clearly defined reallocation of taxing powers so that the provincial governments and municipal councils may have adequate financial resources to carry out their rapidly increasing responsibilities.
There, we have it. It is not an attempt to deprive the provinces, such as Manitoba, of their legitimate share of tax resources. It is an attempt to provide additional access to those funds and the government, in this present measure, has gone some farther step

along the road to recognizing that the members of the official opposition were correct in their analysis of the problem at the time. In his remarks at the resolution stage the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Drew) has this to say, as reported on page 5593 of Hansard for July 16, 1956. He had criticized the general principle of the bill being brought before the house, and he carries on in the following words:
Now, in saying these things following the speech of the Minister of Finance, I wish to make it quite clear that the present formula has some merits in the acceptance of certain very important principles.
Principles are of the utmost importance in this whole business. Skipping a few lines, the Leader of the Opposition said as follows:
The acceptance by the federal government of the place of the provinces and the right of the provinces in the field of income tax, corporation tax, succession duties and other direct taxes is, in itself, a welcome evidence of a return to the position which was always accepted without question over the years between 1867 and 1941, when the wartime tax agreements were signed.
As a result of prodding by the opposition, we have at least made the point that there is this fundamental principle of federalism to be preserved.
Now, I can go farther than the authority of members of parliament and current members of the government in demonstrating this point. Dr. MacGregor Dawson, one of our outstanding constitutional authorities, has on various occasions stressed the importance of maintaining this principle of giving the provinces their rightful prerogatives in the federal scheme of thing?. For example, on page 135 of the revised edition of his book, "The Government of Canada", he says:
If the Canadian plan is to succeed provinces must be given certain minor tax fields over which they have complete control so that their structure will retain a degree of elasticity and they can enjoy some measure of fiscal independence.
That statement coming from a very eminent authority on Canadian constitutional matters is the point that I am trying to emphasize here. The opposition opposes this measure because, like the old agreements, it misses this fundamental point. The minister recognizes its necessity but does not quite implement it in the bill that we have before us.
I do not have to emphasize the importance of retaining the integrity of local government. That has been done over and over again in this debate. If we fail to give the provinces their rightful place it means that an increase in dependence upon the federal government causes a growing loss of power and prestige so far as the provincial government is concerned as a separate government entity and the same process carries over to the municipal governments as well. It is a fundamental 67509-405J
24, 1956	6383
Federal-Provincial Financial Arrangements condition of any healthy democracy that we must preserve the principle of division or distribution of powers. Without a doubt the tragedy that occurred in this house in early June would not have occurred had it not been for the fact that the prestige, the influence and the power of the lesser levels of government-and I use the phrase "lesser levels of government" in the geographic sense-had been undermined as a result of the increasing encroachments which arose primarily during the wartime conditions and which unfortunately have been perpetuated endlessly into the post-war period. Let me repeat, this is the principle the opposition is fighting for and it is a fundamental principle if we are to avoid what has unfortunately happened in this house, a situation that has been decried by the press from one end of the country to the other, and if we are to preserve a healthy state of democracy.
Let me come back to the sort of propaganda that caused me to rise on this occasion. I think it is absolutely unfair, and it is not in the best interest of national unity, to come out with the sort of propaganda which states that the reason we of the official opposition take this position is that we are favouring one section of the country against the other. As far as I am concerned, we are fighting for the fundamental principle of federal democracy. I could have read further from this pamphlet, but perhaps if I read the sort of publicity that tries to arouse regional passions over this important issue that appears from time to time in Manitoba it might make more effectively the point I am trying to make. Here is an advertisement which appeared in the Elkhorn Mercury around August 8, 1953:
Manitoba now receives $23 million yearly under the dominion tax agreement. Drew would scrap this to fatten the money bags of Ontario and Quebec. Dare we take a chance?
That is the sort of propaganda we are up against in Manitoba and I think that what has happened as a result of the stand we took at that time when we were criticized so severely by the government for our unreasonableness is more than justified by what has happened in the changes in the bill now before us. We are hoping that in taking just as adamant a position in dealing with the inadequacies of the present measure before the house, in so far as they fail to include this fundamental principle of federal democracy, we will have some beneficial effect in helping to restore a balanced democracy in Canada. I do not want to go into that any farther. I wanted to be a little more positive and constructive in so far as the areas in which the lower levels of government might

Procedure in Committees be relieved of certain service responsibilities, and thus be in a position to cope more adequately with the tax resources already allocated to them, are concerned. I refer in this regard especially to the tax on real estate at the municipal level of government. But just in passing, since time does not permit me to do more, I would mention that expensive modern road construction-the hon. member for Prince Albert dealt with this at some length-might quite easily under the British North America Act be carried on by the federal authorities if they so desired, and that is one of the expenses that fall heaviest upon the provinces and upon the municipalities. Under the peace, order and good government section of the British North America Act this responsibility could quite easily be delegated to the senior level of government.
There is one more point that Dawson makes that I should like to touch on before I conclude my remarks and it relates to the statement I have just made. Canada in 1956, because of the failure of the federal government to give leadership in highway construction, does not yet have an all-weather road from the east to western Canada. As a westerner, if I want to travel to Manitoba, I must pass through the United States of America, if I am going to have reasonable driving conditions, and this leads me to an item from book 1 of the Rowell-Sirois report.

This is a matter of rare occurrence. As you may have noticed, the Clerk and I have just had a consultation over the matter. As I understand the situation, standing committees, special committees and committees of the whole house, that is committees to study money resolutions, committees to study ways and means, committees to study supply or committees to study bills are all agencies of the house. According to the authorities the rules of the house are to be followed in committee as far as it is possible and in committee of the whole house an appeal under standing order 59 is allowed from any ruling made by the chairman upon report to the house.
If the rules to be followed by standing and special committees are to be the same as those followed in the committee of the whole we can assume that a member of a committee may appeal the ruling of the chairman, and the chairman of the committee, the same as the chairman of the committee of the whole, would report to the house to have the appeal satisfied by the house pronouncing upon it by way of a vote. That was always my understanding and I was just about ready to put the report to the house.
However, the Clerk has a different opinion on the matter and the argument he puts forward is rather cogent. He submits that the assumption that the rules to be followed by standing and select committees are similar to those followed in the committee of the whole house is based on the English rules and in the United Kingdom there is no such thing as an appeal, either in committee of the whole or in standing and special committees. They settle their own affairs without making a report to the house. If that is so, and if I were to present this report to the house, I am told that we would be initiating something which has never happened. The Clerk and the two deputy clerks have looked for a precedent but they cannot find a single case where an appeal from the ruling by a chairman of a committee has been reported to the house in the fashion which has just been followed today.
As I said a moment ago, I thought there was a possibility that this could be done but after having heard the argument which the Clerk made to me a moment ago it seems to me that the house would want to be most careful as to what precedent would be established if it were to insist upon having this

report placed before it. If committees are to communicate with the house, under the rules there is only one time when the house can accept a report from a committee and that is at the beginning of the sitting under the heading "Presenting Reports by Standing and Special Committees".
This report is no different from any other report by a committee. In the first place, according to standing order 15 this .would be the wrong time to receive a report. It is not a report in the sense that a committee would report a bill or recommendations about a matter which had been referred to it. The house may dispense with the rules on certain occasions. In this particular case the appeal was made by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Regier) who is now in the house. Would the hon. member not be satisfied to have the matter dealt with in the committee on banking and commerce so we could avoid establishing a precedent about which we might perhaps feel sorry later on?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would be only too happy to comply with your suggestion. I simply wanted to impose closure on the lobbying of the finance companies. That was my sole purpose and I think we can settle the matter in committee.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order; I should like to make this brief observation. Standing order 59 states:
The standing orders of the house shall be observed in the committees of the whole house so far as may be applicable, except the standing orders as to the seconding of motions-
Then clause 4 reads:
The chairman shall maintain order in the committees of the whole house, deciding all questions of order subject to an appeal to the house;
Citation 428 of Beauchesne's third edition reads:
From the chairman's decision no appeal should be made to the Speaker.
In case of an appeal to the house, it is the duty of the chairman to leave the chair immediately and report in writing the point of order which he has decided. The Speaker must then submit the matter to the determination of the house in the language reported to him and put the question, "That the decision of the chairman be confirmed." No discussion is allowed on the appeal. Should the Speaker be absent, the chairman takes the chair of the house and another member makes the report of appeal to the acting Speaker who will at once submit the question to the house for its decision.
Under the practice followed in connection with appeals from a ruling of the chairman of the whole house, once an appeal has been taken against a ruling the chairman simply rises and makes an immediate report to the
Procedure in Committees Speaker. That does not give rise to the difficulty which you have mentioned of perhaps creating an interruption in the business of the house which might be the case if a select committee were making such report. Nevertheless citation 428 is in broad enough terms to include an appeal from the decision of a chairman of any select committee.
Personally I do not recall any appeal to the house in a situation of this kind, but I do remember an occasion some years ago when an appeal was taken from a chairman's ruling and he ruled that there was no power in the select committee to entertain the appeal and that the appeal must be taken to the house and that he must make a report to the Speaker.
The Speaker does not rule on the appeal. He simply puts the question to the house, and in the light of citation 428 I should have thought that was clearly the proper practice.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether I might say a word in support of the arguments which you say have been made to you by the Clerk of the house. It seems to me that the Clerk is quite right in suggesting that this would be a new precedent if the house were to consider the appeal from the ruling of the chairman of the banking and commerce committee. The hon. member for Eglinton has drawn your attention to citation 428. I suggest, however, that citation 428 clearly relates to what happens when there is an appeal from the chairman of the committee of the whole house. I draw the attention of the hon. member for Eglinton to citation 534, which is under the chapter in Beauchesne's third edition having to do with standing committees, in which it says:
Committees are regarded as portions of the House and are governed for the most part in their proceedings by the same rules which prevail in the House.
In both instances "House" is spelled with a capital "H". I suggest that this is clear. The next sentence is:
Every question is determined in a committee in the same manner as in the House to which it belongs.
"House" is spelled with a capital "H" again. I suggest that that makes it clear that the proceedings of a standing committee are governed by the rules and the practices that prevail in the house, not in a committee of the whole house, and in the house we would deal with an appeal from the Speaker's ruling, if such were sought, by a vote of the members of the house. Similarly, I think we would be not only meeting the request of the member for Burnaby-Coquitlam but we would be doing the right thing if we referred

Procedure in Committees this matter back to the committee on banking and commerce and let the members of that committee make the decision as to whether or not they support the ruling of the chairman. In addition to citation 534 in Beau-chesne's third edition, may I refer to certain citations in Beauchesne's second edition? First of all, there is citation 602, which is substantially the same as citation 534 in his third edition. Then on the next page I note citation 607, which states:
Committees are governed in their proceedings by the same rules which prevail in the House and which continue in lull operation in every select committee. It is upon this principle, that the practice appears to be founded, of consulting the Speaker, in reference to points of order and the forms of proceedings, by select committees.
There^ is quite a difference between the provisions in standing order 59 for an appeal to the house from a committee of the whole house and what is spelled out in citation 607, namely, consultation with the Speaker. In the other case, on which Your Honour had occasion to rule some weeks ago, the Speaker does not come into the picture at all; he merely puts the vote. So far as these standing committees are concerned, is it not quite clear from citation 607 that if the hon. member for Parkdale is in doubt as to what he should do he can have a consultation with Your Honour, but that that does not need to be in the house? I submit that we would be doing the right thing if we met the request of the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam and referred the matter back to the committee. I think the Clerk of the house has given Your Honour good advice in this respect.

In regard to what the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) has said, the procedure on appeals from a decision of the chairman of the standing committee should be similar to the rule applying to an appeal from a decision of the chairman of the house when sitting as committee of the whole. I thought it might help Your Honour to come to a decision if I cited from Bourinot's third edition, which I happen to have here, pages 519 and 520:
If a question of order arise the chairman will decide it himself, unless it be deemed more advisable to refer the matter to the Speaker in the house itself. Rule 76 provides:
"Questions of order arising in committee of the whole house shall be decided by the chairman, subject to an appeal to the house; but disorder in a committee can only be censured by the house, on receiving a report thereof."
In case of an appeal to the house it is the duty of the chairman of the committee to report in writing the point of order which he has decided. The Speaker must then submit the matter to the determination of the house in the language reported


to him, and put the question-"That the decision of the chairman be confirmed." No discussion is allowed on the appeal.
I respectfully submit that, our two authorities on parliamentary procedure, Beauchesne and Bourinot, not forgetting the hon. member for Eglinton, being of the same opinion, there should be no discussion on that.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is interesting to find the hon. member for Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Cannon) taking the view that he does. Just as he rose I was about to rise and direct your attention to at least two precedents on which I have been able to put my hands in regard to appeals from chairmen's rulings. This is in regard to a special committee, it is true, not a standing committee, but I think the procedure is the same whereby appeals from chairmen's rulings were decided by a vote of the committee. The hon. member was a member of that committee and voted to sustain the chairman's ruling in each case. It was not referred to the house, and nobody suggested that it be referred to the house.
I must confess I am surprised that the point should have arisen, because I have served on numbers of committees, both standing and select committees, where the chairman's ruling has been appealed and the matter has been settled by a vote of the committee without any suggestion being made that the appeal should be referred to the house. I refer to these two examples. In the special committee on estimates last year, you will find in the reports of Wednesday, March 2, and Friday, March 11, appeals from the chairman's ruling on that committee. I think we had more than two such appeals, but those are the two I have been able to turn up quickly.
I recall that in another select committee, it is true, the committee on veterans affairs in 1945 and 1946, there were a few occasions when there were appeals from a chairman's ruling. I also recall that in the special committee on defence expenditures we had appeals from the chairman's rulings, and they were decided in the committee.
Those committees to which I have referred were under experienced chairmen: in two cases the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Tucker) and in another case the former member for Spadina, now a member of the Senate; and that is the practice that was followed almost automatically. It did not occur to any member of those committees for a moment that it would have to be referred to the house. I should think that is because of a provision in a citation to which my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre has

referred, that the proceedings in committee, meaning the standing and select committees, are governed by the proceedings in the house, spelled with a capital "h", meaning therefore the house in a technical sense, where an appeal from the Speaker's ruling would be decided by a vote. So in committee an appeal from the chairman's ruling, I suggest, should be decided by a vote of the members of that committee. Otherwise there will be, as somebody has pointed out, constant interruptions to the proceedings of the house.
