speechtext: As the hon. member has referred to me, I might be allowed a word in reply. It is by unanimous consent of the committee in question if an appeal is made from the chairman's ruling to the committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: REFERENCE TO HOUSE OF APPEAL FROM RULING OF CHAIRMAN OF COMMITTEE
speechtext:
I might say that it is music to my ears to hear hon. members plead that when an appeal is made from the chairman's ruling the Speaker must put the report immediately to the house and, according to citation 428, have it disposed of. I could not agree more with the opinion of the hon. member for Eglinton and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre on that score. I am only sorry that I did not adhere to those opinions at all times. It is almost with tears in my eyes that I recall the experience that cost me so much.
If we are to assume that the rules are to the effedit that the rules in committee of the whole apply to the proceedings in standing committees and if in consequence of that the chairman, having received an appeal, acted upon the wording of citation 428 of Beau-chesne, third edition, he had no alternative but to leave the chair and do as he has done. It appears to me that in the first place this is not the proper time to present such a report because, according to standing order 15, it should be done at the beginning of our proceedings.
In the second place, the practice has been ascertained both by the Clerk and by experienced members of the house and, as particularly pointed out by the hon. member for Kamloops, who said he had found two examples where appeals had been settled within the committee itself. I would gather that the practice with respect to appeals in standing and special committees is to have them settled by the committee itself.
Third, I think the house should consider the point raised by the Clerk which is to the effect that our practice is based largely on what happens in the United Kingdom. There appeals are not settled by the house. As a matter of fact, they have no appeals in their committees. They take the decisions made by the chairman without appealing.
I also go along with the remarks made by the hon. member for Kamloops to the effect that if we were to initiate this procedure of having appeals heard by the house there would be no end to the disturbances which might thereby be created, and I do not think that we create committees to study special matters that we refer to them merely for the purpose of having the chairman come back here and interrupt our proceedings in order to take a division on every one of the appeals which may be taken from the rulings of a committee chairman.


As I have said, it is against my own preference to make a ruling now but I am informed, and I know that it is so, that the committee cannot continue to function unless and until I give a ruling. I would have much preferred to study the matter more carefully and give a ruling later. In making a ruling now, however, I will enter this caveat, that I will study the matter further and should I find that I am wrong I will come to the house and say so. I have to rule now that the appeal from the chairman's ruling should be settled in the committee on banking and commerce and not reported to this house.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, February 28, consideration of the motion of Mr. Diefenbaker for the second reading of Bill No. 66, to amend the Criminal Code (nuisance).

speakeroldname: Hon. Stuart S. Garson (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING POLLUTION OF INTERPROVINCIAL RIVERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) moved the second reading of this bill on February 28 last, I was not able to rise to reply to his case until just a few minutes before six o'clock. In those few minutes I pointed out that we in the government were deeply sympathetic with the objectives which my hon. friend had in mind, but that we gravely doubted the efficacy of the method he proposed to use to achieve them.
The whole question here, of course, is as to what is the best method of solving this problem of pollution. As I have stated on previous occasions on which we have considered this matter, I do not think a satisfactory solution to this problem can be found by proceedings in the criminal courts. That, of course, has been the view of the government all along and it is still our view.
The impression I gained from these remarks of the hon. member for Prince Albert is that the supposed need for his introducing this amendment to the Criminal Code arises from what, in my opinion, he mistakenly regards as a defect in the existing law.
I think he is also mistaken in that, if such a defect existed,-and I do not think it does exist-the amendment which he has moved would not remedy this alleged defect. That is my submission, and I will now attempt to show that it is well founded.
Now, it may be that I do not understand correctly the case of my hon. friend from Prince Albert. In order to make sure that we are ad idem-that we understand one

another-I should like to attempt to recapitulate his case in the hon. member's presence and to ask him to correct me if, at any stage, I state his position wrongly.
First, he made the plea, on the basis of a quotation by the mayor of Prince Albert of an opinion obtained from Mr. McCuaig of Edmonton, that there was "the legal difficulty of a city in one province obtaining an injunction against a city in another province and stated that as yet he has found no legal method by which this "can be accomplished", that is to say there was no legal method by which an injunction could be obtained in Alberta in respect to a common nuisance which had been created in Prince Albert in Saskatchewan. Then having pointed out that that civil remedy was not available, the hon. member for Prince Albert went on to say this, and I am now quoting from page 1633 of Hansard of February 28, 1956:
Having first pointed out that the person has no civil rights on an interprovincial river whose water supply has been polluted. I am now endeavouring, following that, to show that the only means is to put teeth in the criminal law so that wrongdoers who would take advantage of the situation and thereby destroy this bounty of nature shall be severely punished.
Then my hon. friend goes on to say what his conception of the law is at the present time, a conception with which I shall in due course take issue. He states it in these terms on page 1634 of Hansard:
As the law stands today there is no right under section 165, the present nuisance section, or any other section of the Criminal Code, to prosecute wrongdoers on interprovincial rivers. All that section will do is to cover the individual who dumps a bit of stuff into a river within the province in which the prosecution takes place. But nowhere and under no authority can anything be done by people living in provinces adjoining the province in which the pollution has taken place.
At that point I intervened with this question:
Under the amendment to the code which he proposes,-
That is the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker).
-if someone in Edmonton were guilty of an offence under it. which offence caused difficulty in Prince Albert, would he not agree that the prosecution of that offence would have to be conducted by the Alberta law enforcement authorities?
To that question my hon. friend from Prince Albert replied in part as follows:
I do not have before me the section of the Criminal Code that covers exactly that type of thing where an offence happens affecting two jurisdictions.
Later, Mr. Speaker, I will cite that section to which the hon. gentleman was presumably referring and will endeavour to show that it completely covers the problem that he had in mind. He continued as follows:
Criminal Code
One of the earlier general sections of the Criminal Code provides for eventualities similar to that; but whether or not my hon. friend is correct, suppose the pollution took place in the province of Alberta: all that would need to be done would be for a charge to be laid in the province of Alberta and the witnesses transported to the place of trial within Alberta.
In other words, in those remarks my hon. friend from Prince Albert indicated that he had the impression, in perhaps a somewhat inchoate form but nevertheless a correct impression, of what the law is at the present time. Then I asked this question:
May I ask my hon. friend another question? If that be so, then would not the same condition of affairs and the same reason apply to a charge for committing a common nuisance which had been committed in Alberta, which caused a bad effect in Prince Albert and which could be prosecuted in Alberta by taking Saskatchewan witnesses to Alberta for that purpose?
My hon. friend's reply to that question was this:
With that general proposition I am not in agreement. In making pollution on interprovincial rivers a criminal offence I think the prosecution could be taken in either place where the pollution actually took place or in the province in which the effects of that pollution were felt.
Then after quoting from the definition of what is a common nuisance under law as it is now, the hon. member for Prince Albert goes on to say this:
If the section as it now stands covered such cases as this, then a person in Prince Albert or any other place in Saskatchewan affected by the pollution would be able to take a prosecution against the Alberta company. But as the law now stands there is no provision whatsoever.
That is the point upon which I take issue with my hon. friend. The hon. gentleman from Prince Albert continued:
That is not my opinion, although I entirely concur in it: that is the opinion of counsel. Under the law as it now stands, there is nothing that can be done by a resident in one province to meet the nuisance of pollution in an adjoining province.
Then I again intervened with a question as follows:
Would he-
That is the hon. gentleman from Prince Albert:
Would he point out in his amendment the provision therein which makes it possible for a person in Saskatchewan to prosecute an offender in Alberta? What language in his amendment provides for that possibility?
That is to say, if the supposed defect in the existing law is that a man who suffers a nuisance in Prince Albert cannot prosecute in Alberta, I was asking my hon. friend what it was in his amendment-that is the one that is now under discussion-that would remedy that defect. My hon. friend's reply thereto was as follows:
Just wait a minute. I have already said that under the section as it now stands proceedings

Criminal Code
could be taken in Prince Albert if the present nuisance section covered the situation. I say that it does not cover that situation because pollution of an interprovincial stream does not come within the law as it is now constituted. It is because of that fact that I want this amendment added so as to cover interprovincial streams. Then immediately there will be available the right of action and there will also be teeth in the law.
So, Mr. Speaker, upon that point, the question of whether or not my hon. friend has a case depends upon whether he is right in his statement that there is no provision in the law to enable a person suffering from a nuisance committed in one province to prosecute in another. I would refer him in that connection to section 419 of the Criminal Code. I think this is the one that he had in mind when he said that there was a provision in the code covering cases "where an offence happens affecting two jurisdictions". Section 419 reads as follows:
419. For the purpose of this act,
(a)	where an offence is committed in or upon any water or upon a bridge, between two or more territorial divisions, the offence shall be deemed to have been committed in any of the territorial divisions;
(b)	where an offence is committed on the boundary of two or more territorial divisions or within 500 yards of any such boundary, or the offence was commenced within one territorial division and completed within another, the offence shall be deemed to have been committed in any of the territorial divisions.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I apprehend that where, in the province of Alberta, a company or companies or municipality, under the existing criminal law, discharge a polluting effluent into the Saskatchewan river which going down that river constitutes when it reaches Prince Albert, a common nuisance within the meaning of the relevant section of the code, that is a case which clearly falls within section 419(b). There is, therefore, no necessity for my hon. friend to move his present amendment for the purpose of clearing up that difficulty. It is already cleared up in this section 419 of the code. But if it had not been cleared up already in the code, then my hon. friend's amendment would not have had that effect in any case; because if this difficulty had existed the mere reference in my hon. friend's amendment to an interprovincial river would not have the effect of meeting this alleged difficulty.
Then, my hon. friend from Prince Albert goes on; and this is his next objection, as set out at page 1635 of Hansard for February 28, 1956:
As the matter stands today the maximum penalty-even if the present section applied-on indictment is two years or the matter could be proceeded with by way of summary conviction in which case the maximum penalty would be $500. But $500 penalties, even if they were applicable,
[Mr. Garson.1
would be simply nothing to corporations which wantonly and wilfully pollute these waters.
I go back to this principle and I am trying to make it clear to my hon. friend. As the law is now, or as the section reads now, there is no right of action for the pollution of international rivers. The amendment will make it an offence.
Now, with regard to this matter of penalties, I would refer my hon. friend to section 623 of the code which reads as follows:
Notwithstanding subsection (2) of section 621-
A reference which has no bearing upon the use of this section in the present context.
-a corporation that is convicted of an offence is liable, in lieu of any imprisonment that is prescribed as punishment for that offence,
(a) to be fined in an amount that is in the discretion of the court, where the offence is an indictable offence,-
So that the whole of my hon. friend's argument that the penalties under the relevant section of the Criminal Code are inadequate for the type of offence that was envisaged here is quite unfounded. If an accused were a corporation and were found guilty of this offence, which is an indictable offence, then there is no limit at all to the amount of the penalty which the court could impose.
Now, Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend's position it seems to me is that he wants an amendment to the law because he is under the impression, which with respect I think is an incorrect impression, that the present law is not effective or not applicable. He says he has an opinion to that effect, but he did not table it or quote it except in very general terms. In my judgment that opinion is wrong. It may be that I am wrong in this matter; and if that were so then until these points are decided by the courts we would not know which of the two views was correct, although in the face of these clear provisions I have just quoted it does seem to me that the matter is not susceptible of very much doubt.
But I would state this, that both in provincial legislatures and in this house where a given law seems to require some reform the practice is the one which we followed in the revision of the Criminal Code, to have the need for reform studied, to draft legislation, to enact legislation with such amendments as may be made by committees of the house or by the house itself, and then when the law has been passed not to amend it further until it has been interpreted by the courts in a way that for example in the present case would afford my hon. friend some legitimate foundation for his suggestion that the law should be further changed.
Until the sections of the code which I have quoted today, which seem to me to be crystal clear, have been held by the courts not to mean what they say, I do not think my hon.

Criminal Code
friend should come to this house with the suggestion that it be changed upon the basis of the sort of argument he has made in support of the change or of the information he has collected in support of this argument.
As I have said on previous occasions, we on this side of the house do not think a solution of this problem of the contamination of the waters of the country can be reached by any kind of criminal court method. I am not suggesting we should repeal any of the existing provisions which have stood the test of time, but I think if we are thoughtful we all realize that pollution is going to be cured by doing away with it by concerted efforts upon the part of the responsible governments concerned.
In order to inform the house as to steps that have been taken during this past year since the last time I made a report in this regard in relation to the North Saskatchewan river-

speechtext:
I should like to illustrate this, and then I shall be glad to answer the question after that. An eminent counsel in the United States was examining a medical expert of national standing before a jury. He said to the medical expert, "Do you know Mr. Jones?" "Yes." During routine sampling carried out by the provincial department of health of Alberta in the early months of 1956, odours which were described as stale or septic were noted. This condition was quite distinct from that which gave rise to complaints during the winter of 1953-54. This condition was attributed to lack of oxygen resulting

Criminal Code
from the pollution originating in and near Edmonton and aggravated by the fact that the stream was ice-covered.
In an attempt to correct the situation, the Alberta health authorities instituted mechanical aeration of the stream, some 60 to 80 miles below Edmonton. Owing to difficulties of a mechanical nature and the lateness of the season, this experiment could only be continued for about three weeks. Consequently, only a slight increase in the oxygen content of the river was obtained. The equipment used in this experiment was supplied by the city of Edmonton and had been out of service for several years. When the electric motors were put into service, they burned out and some time was lost in replacing them. Comparatively mild weather during the experiment resulted in the ice remaining open at the points where it had been broken to instal the aeration tubes. Consequently, much of the air escaped through these openings.
Carbon filter studies carried out at the same time and with the assistance of the United States public health service and the Ontario department of health were designed to identify the pollutants responsible for odours. Examination of the extracts obtained from the carbon filters are now being conducted in the laboratories of the Alberta research council.
It should be noted that by means of observations and analyses conditions in the North Saskatchewan river are being checked constantly by the Alberta health department. It it our understanding that the oxygen content of the North Saskatchewan river has returned to normal as a result of the spring breakup with no complaints of odour.
The available information indicates that water treatment plants taking water from the North Saskatchewan river were able to produce water of satisfactory quality during the past several months.
Industries in the Edmonton area are continuing to maintain effective control of their wastes. For example, it is known that certain procedures, such as the following, have been instituted: burning of high-odour wastes, using combustible wastes as fuel and the retention of potentially offensive wastes which are checked prior to release to the river, or discharged to holding ponds if they are found to be objectionable. Storage ponds are used extensively to retain and dissipate wastes which might contribute unsatisfactory conditions in the river. Thus it can be noted that the industries of the Edmonton area have been active in providing treatment facilities for the control of taste and odour-producing wastes capable of producing objectionable conditions in the North Saskatchewan river. Results have been gratifying.
The city of Edmonton has been actively engaged in providing treatment plants for its municipal wastes in order to comply with the requirements of the provincial health department. A sewage treatment plant to provide primary treatment for part of the city's sewage was put into operation in 1955. Secondary treatment facilities are presently being provided at this plant. A second sewage treatment plant is now under construction and this will provide primary treatment for the balance of the city's wastes. These facilities should be in operation in the autumn of 1956. It is understood that this program will be continued so that secondary treatment of all the city's wastes will be achieved within the near future. This will obviously improve conditions in the river to a marked degree.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that my hon. friend himself will agree there is more in that one statement in the way of progress in the control of the pollution of the North Saskatchewan river than my hon. friend can achieve in

a dozen criminal prosecutions, whether under the existing law or under the amendment which he has moved and which I think is totally unnecessary.

National security, national development and the fostering of trade and commerce by appropriate regulation were regarded by the fathers-
By that they mean the founding fathers. -as the great functions of government. They were also the functions which they thought likely to expand in the future. When these had been transferred to the federal government, the provinces were left with functions, the burden of which was not expected to grow.
I think that gets us to the main part of our problem. The federal government assumed the major responsibilities of national security, national development and the fostering of trade and commerce. As the committee rose at five o'clock I was stating that notwithstanding the rapid development in this country in the past two decades, particularly since world war II, we have not yet built an allCanadian highway from east to west. That is symptomatic of general neglect of the functions of national development allotted to the federal government.

One reason for the necessity of tax rental agreements, equalization payments and so forth arises from the neglect of the development of national economy in various parts of the country. I decided to raise this point because in the house today we heard some statesmanlike utterances concerning depressions and such like and the responsibilities pertaining thereto. Such speeches are often made in this house and there is not always a strict regard for historical accuracy.
If there is any cause for complaint concerning the progress of the development of the nation it certainly does not fall upon the shoulders of Her Majesty's loyal opposition, because since 1896 we have had the privilege of holding office only for some sixteen years. The Liberal party has carried the burden of responsibility for most of that entire period. Therefore if there is any criticism as to the state of the development of our economy it rests squarely upon the shoulders of that party.
Accusations are made concerning depressions and 20 cents per day. That was a measure adopted to meet an emergency problem in connection with young men who were unemployed during that period. I left college in 1937 two years after a Liberal administration had been returned to power and we were still in the depths of very serious depression. speechtext: This is the important clause which provides for the fiscal needs of those provinces which do not share the benefits of confederation as fully as some of the others. That is a principle which has been generally endorsed by all parties. Certainly our opposition to the bill did not indicate in any sense opposition to the principle of equalization payments. I think it would be well to point out as this clause is being considered that this formula which has been developed is a pretty rough measure of the fiscal needs of a province. In fact, it is not a formula based on fiscal needs at all. It is a formula based on the difference between the value of three taxes to a province compared with the value of those same three taxes in the provinces of Ontario and British Columbia at this time. Therefore it is really a formula which provides for payments based on the means of a province rather than on its needs, if I may make that distinction, and although it undoubtedly equalizes the revenues in these three tax fields among the provinces and to that extent does meet fiscal needs I do leave the thought with the house that this is not a scientific method, if I may say so, of arriving at what has been generally subscribed to as the necessity for equalizing payments among the provinces to enable them to provide a minimum or average standard of services to their people throughout the country.

Mr. Chairman, looking at subclause 3 of clause 6 we find that it says:
The minister, with the approval of the governor in council, may, on behalf of the government of Canada, enter into an agreement, not inconsistent with the provisions of this act, amending the terms and conditions of a tax rental agreement.
I call attention to that power because of the history of previous tax rental agreements and to say that I hope that this is not looking forward to a series of bargains different one from the other in which one province may obtain an advantage which then is requested by other provinces and the agreements then cease to follow a pattern which at least holds an even balance but change from time to time.
I recall to the minister the sequence of events immediately after 1946 when Mr. Ilsley's budget gave authority somewhat similar to this and three provinces entered into agreements. I think they were Alberta, Saskatchewan and one of the maritime provinces. Then, British Columbia, presenting some very powerful arguments, secured what were undoubtedly much better terms from the federal authorities. That, of course, set


the whole thing off again and there was a clamour from those who had signed wanting the same terms, and so the process of bargaining went on.
I am not sure what the purpose is of this provision which permits amendment in the course of the five years. Presumably the agreements will be made according to the terms of this legislation, that is, according to the formula which has been devised, and will be the same for all of the provinces and devised to do substantial justice at this level of tax sharing for which the legislation provides. If that is so, perhaps the minister would indicate what he has in mind in taking the power to amend uniform agreements which he looks forward to signing with a number of provinces in the course of the five year period.

I believe that since 1952 we have only amended one agreement once and that was with respect to certain logging taxes in British Columbia. The other provinces, of course, were aware of this and they felt as we did, that it was a problem peculiar to British Columbia and that, if we felt so, it was a proper way of amending that particular agreement. speechtext: In the first place, Mr. Chairman, the provincial government would have to impose the tax in question; in the second place, it would have to be a tax with respect to which the definitions and exemptions were substantially the same as our own; and in the third place, they would have to agree to pay us a modest fee for collecting.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: We have made no arrangements, of course, because up to the present time no province has indicated anything more than academic interest in this proposal, and we have not suggested any particular fee. It would be negotiated with the provincial government. During the conference we made it clear that it was not our desire to make any profit out of this matter but that we would want to retain out of the tax about the cost of collecting. While I would let the provincial premiers speak for themselves on this matter, I think that most of them felt that we could collect probably as cheaply as could they. I think the house will understand that if the tax law happened to be substantially different from our own there would be a great many difficulties in collection and therefore we would not undertake it.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: If the province has tax laws substantially the same, its variation in rate from the standard rates permitted in the act will not prevent that province from having its taxes collected by the federal authority? For example, what I have in mind is this. Under the arrangements which existed before the war I think the federal government collected personal income taxes for the province of Ontario and also for the province of British Columbia, with the result that the taxpayer had only one return to file, the taxes were paid to one authority and then distributed, and the province was free to levy whatever rate of tax it saw fit to levy. Will that flexibility exist under this legislation, Mr. Chairman? For example, can a province levy an income tax which is more than the authorized ten percentage points and still have it collected by the federal authority if the terms of exemption and so on of the taxing statute are substantially the same?

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES

But as I said at the resolution stage of this bill, five years is a long time, although not nearly as long as the 20-year period to which some hon. members kept referring in the course of the debate; and one never knows what will come out over a period of time as a result of consideration by the various governments. subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR AGREEMENTS WITH PROVINCES
speechtext: I hope the government has not come to any final decision in these matters because it seems to me-and this opinion has been expressed by various speakers on the other side-that there is a real advantage in not requiring duplicate sets of returns. It seems to me to be consistent with the principle of freedom of a taxing authority among the provincial authorities that the federal government should act as an agent where the tax laws are substantially the same except in the matter of rate. After all, that is the point we have been arguing. The decision as to the rate of tax in these fields is the responsibility of the province as an autonomous government with an equal authority in that field. I now express the hope that the government will show that degree of co-operation which is essential in a federal system in working out arrangements to meet the circumstances which arise in the future where there are differences as to the rate of tax to be collected and where provinces see fit to go their own way within the reasonable limits of this taxsharing proposal.

the second reading of Bill No. 439, to amend the Indian Act.
He said: I have no intention of speaking at any great length on the second reading of this bill. There was considerable debate at 67509-406$
Indian Act
the resolution stage and a number of points were raised which I think could perhaps, more appropriately in most cases, be dealt with on my estimates, if and when they are reached. Most of them had very little relationship to the contents of the bill. I make no pretensions for this bill. I did not at the resolution stage, and I do not now. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris), when he had the portfolio I now have the honour to have, brought before this house a complete revision of the Indian Act. After two years' experience as minister, it is my opinion that this parliament did an excellent job in revising that act and that several years should go by before any major revisions are made.
The hon. member for Prince Albert, speaking at the resolution stage, suggested that the time had come to establish a royal commission to consider the future of the Canadian Indians. I would not say, out of hand, that I was opposed to that recommendation but I would say that I think it is a little too soon to do it. I think we need a few more years' experience with the kind of limited self government for the Indians that was instituted when the act was revised in 1951, and that produced the results which I attempted to describe to the house at the resolution stage of this bill.
Now, one purpose of this bill is to tidy up a few points that, in the course of administration, proved not to be quite as well drafted as perhaps it was thought they were when the act was passed in 1951. These are what I would call housekeeping amendments, and I do not really intend to say anything about them on the second reading. I will be quite prepared to explain any of them that do not explain themselves, and I think most of them do, when we get into the committee.
There are a number of clauses verifying Indian status, the two most important of which relate to children. There is some importance in them, and they do recognize a new principle and I think a good principle. It is unfortunately true that all too frequently Indian women have children before they are married. Some of these children are children whose paternity seems to be in a good deal of doubt. Up to now, the law has provided that an effort must be made to establish their paternity before they can be put on the rolls of the band. This has caused some hardship which I think has been unfortunate. I found at the meeting with the representatives of the Indians in December that there was not universal agreement, but that the overwhelming majority of the representatives felt that these children ought to be put on

Indian Act
the band lists and be subject to protest within a certain period. It seems to me that is a much more humane way to deal with the problem.
There is another section dealing with the children of Indian women who marry non-Indians. As the law stands at present, Indian women who marry non-Indians are iinmediately-I should not say immediately but as soon as the governor in council can get around to it-enfranchised and cease to have Indian status. It has been the custom, and it is indeed the law, to enfranchise compulsorily the minor children of Indian women who marry non-Indians. That is quite all right in most cases where the children go to live as non-Indians with the stepfather. It works no hardship and it is indeed probably the right thing in most cases to do that. But in some cases these children remain on the reserve with grandparents or other relatives and live as Indians. It is the intention in the future that the enfranchisement of these children will not be compulsory but will be optional, depending Upon the circumstances.
At the resolution stage I dealt at some length with the revolving fund which is, of course, the only section of the bill which has any financial implications, and I see no need to repeat anything I said at that time.
There are certain other clauses in the bill which have economic but no financial effects. There are clauses for the facilitating of the leasing of Indian lands where the Indians want to lease them. There are clauses making it easier to use the capital of bands for housing, to permit the pledging of band credit for housing loans and to authorize borrowing by bands for band projects and housing.
Now, I found that there were a minority of the Indians, a quite substantial minority, particularly those who were engaged in farming in western Canada, who felt that it would be desirable to go quite a lot farther and give them exactly the same rights as other people to pledge their lands and their other possessions in order to get credit. I must say I had a good deal of sympathy for the point of view they expressed; but it was quite clear that the majority of the Indians at the conference were not in favour of doing that. They feared it meant that something was going to be taken away from them, and we came rather reluctantly to the conclusion that this was such a step that, although some of the Indians were ready for it, they would have to wait for another occasion.
I have not any doubt-although I wish it were not so-that the parts of this legislation
[Mr. Pickersgill.l
which will be debated most, both in this chamber and outside, are those clauses relating to the proposed changes in the law with respect to intoxicating beverages, and perhaps I might explain very briefly, first, what the present situation is and then what is now proposed.
A really fundamental change was made when the act was amended in 1951 and when for the first time it was left to any provincial authority which wished to do it to take certain initiatives which would result in permitting Indians in that province to consume alcoholic beverages in public places, but no other aspect of the provincial liquor laws could be made to apply to Indians. Several of the provinces have taken advantage of that provision of the law: British Columbia, Nova Scotia, Ontario, the Yukon Territory, and, most recently of all, the province of Manitoba. In fact, I think it was only one day last week that the provision came into effect in Manitoba.
What we are proposing at this time in this legislation is to extend the law in two directions. We are providing for a provincial initiative which would make it possible for the Indians in a province to be brought under all the liquor laws of the province, but the initiative would have to be taken by the provincial government. There is this further proviso, that any band which by a majority of its membership decides not to come under the general law could establish a form of local option on the reserve.
Then, we are also proposing, because I have been advised that there are one or two provincial governments which take the view that they would not object to having this discrimination done away with, though they do not feel they ought to take the initiative, for the initiative to be taken by the band on a particular reserve. In that case we would carry out their wishes only if the provincial authorities, having been apprised of their views on this subject, did not object. We feel that, since the provincial authorities have the responsibility for the administration of the liquor laws in the province, we should not go the whole length of abolishing the present law and imposing an entirely new regime without some measure of provincial consent. I suppose there will be members of the house who will say we should have gone the whole hog and had complete non-discrimination and there will be others who will say-in fact some hon. members have said to me privately-that they object to our giving liquor to the Indians. On that point I want to say just a word.
There is no intention on the part of the government of giving any liquor to the

Indians or to anybody else. All this bill will do is to enable some Indians in some parts of Canada, after certain initiatives are taken, to buy liquor legally instead of doing as I am afraid is the fact, as I know-let us not pretend about this-far too many of them do now, that is buy it illegally.
There is another provision in the bill which I think I ought to refer to briefly and that is the section in regard to education. This section gives the minister the authority to require, rather than to permit, Indian children to go to school. I think this is something on which there would be unanimity in the house.
Really, sir, I would not have said anything else about this bill had not a point been raised at the resolution stage which I feel it is necessary for me to refer to. I refer to the fact that at four or five places in this bill the word "minister" is substituted for the words "governor in council". Because of that, an attempt was made by several members of the official opposition at the resolution stage to suggest, because evidently they had heard some rumours about what was likely to be in the bill, that this in some way was an attempt at self-glorification by the minister or an expansion of his powers, at whose expense I was not quite clear. Now, sir, I think it would take me 10 or 15 minutes to complete what I have to say and I am willing

to go ahead if hon. members wish me to do so, or I am willing to move the adjournment of the debate.
